questions.prompt: A test case for an agent needs three things. Which set is right?

options.text: A prompt, a model id, and a temperature
An initial state, an input, and an expected result
A trace id, a severity, and an owner
A judge prompt, a dev split, and a test split

explanations.a: Those describe a configuration, not a test. Two configurations can run the same test.
explanations.b: Correct. Freeze the world (initial state), freeze what the customer says (input), and write down what correct means (expected). Drop one and the case cannot be replayed.
explanations.c: Those fields belong on a review sheet from Lesson 4, not on a test case.
explanations.d: Those are the pieces of validating a judge. A test case may reference a pinned judge, but it is not one.

questions.prompt: Which failure should become a code assertion, and which a pinned judge check?

options.text: Assertion: "wrong tone"; judge: "refund amount over order total"
Assertion: "refund amount over order total"; judge: "wrong tone"
Both should be judges, because tests should be flexible
Both should be assertions, because judges are too slow

explanations.a: Backwards. Tone needs interpretation; an amount comparison does not.
explanations.b: Correct. Mechanical failures get code assertions (free, deterministic). Subjective failures get a judge whose prompt and model version are pinned.
explanations.c: Flexibility is the enemy of a regression test. Use code wherever the verdict is mechanical.
explanations.d: An assertion cannot decide whether a reply sounds dismissive. Pin a judge for those, and run it on the tier that can afford it.

questions.prompt: What does it mean to "pin" a judge in a CI suite?

options.text: Run it on every commit
Freeze its prompt and its model version so a change in the result means the agent changed, not the judge
Give it the highest severity
Let it see the test split so it stays calibrated

explanations.a: How often it runs is a cost-tier decision, not what pinning means.
explanations.b: Correct. If the judge itself moves, you cannot tell whether a red build is the agent's fault. Pin both the prompt and the model id.
explanations.c: Severity is a property of the failure mode, not of the judge.
explanations.d: Never. A judge that has seen the test split is burned (Lesson 5).

questions.prompt: Which cost tier runs on every commit, and why?

options.text: Tier 2, full agent evals with a real model, because they are the most realistic
Tier 0, deterministic code checks, because they cost nothing and finish in milliseconds
Tier 1, mocked tools, because they catch tool bugs
All tiers, so nothing slips through

explanations.a: Realistic and expensive. Run the full evals on pull requests or nightly, not on every keystroke.
explanations.b: Correct. Free and instant checks can run constantly. The expensive tiers run less often, on a schedule that matches their cost.
explanations.c: Mocked integration is cheap enough for every pull request, but the every-commit tier is the deterministic one.
explanations.d: Running dollars of model calls on every commit burns budget and slows everyone down. Match frequency to cost.

questions.prompt: Sprout answers an order-status question correctly with probability 0.95. A customer asks once. Which number tells you what that customer will experience, and what is it for k = 3 runs?

options.text: pass@3, about 0.9999
pass^3, about 0.857
pass@3, about 0.857
pass^3, about 0.95

explanations.a: pass@3 says at least one of three tries succeeds. The customer does not get three tries.
explanations.b: Correct. pass^3 = 0.95 x 0.95 x 0.95 = 0.857: the chance all three replays are right, which is the reliability a one-shot customer feels.
explanations.c: The value is right for pass^3, but pass@3 is the wrong name and the wrong idea.
explanations.d: 0.95 is the single-run probability. pass^3 multiplies it three times.

questions.prompt: Why does reset-and-replay reset the world before each replay?

options.text: To make the model deterministic
Because state from one run (a cancelled order, a queued refund) would leak into the next and change the result
To clear the prompt cache
Because judges require an empty database

explanations.a: Resetting the world does not change how the model samples. It keeps the inputs identical.
explanations.b: Correct. If run 1 cancels order #1077, run 2 starts with a cancelled order and measures a different scenario. Reset, replay, count failures.
explanations.c: Prompt caching is a cost feature (Lesson 9) and is unrelated to test isolation.
explanations.d: Judges read traces. They do not care about the database. The agent does.

questions.prompt: With p = 0.8 and k = 3, compute pass^3 and pass@3 (show the arithmetic), and explain which one a support agent needs and why.
rubric: States that a support agent needs pass^k because each customer gets one attempt and the number measures reliability
States that pass@k measures capability (at least one success) and is the wrong number for a customer-facing agent
questions.modelAnswer: pass^3 = 0.8 x 0.8 x 0.8 = 0.512. pass@3 = 1 - (0.2 x 0.2 x 0.2) = 1 - 0.008 = 0.992. A support agent needs pass^k: Alex asks once and gets one answer, so what matters is the chance the agent is right every time, which is 51% here even though the single-run rate looks like 80%. pass@k only says the agent can get it right in at least one of three tries, which measures capability, not what the customer receives.

questions.prompt: Write a test case in YAML for the failure mode *Refund outside policy*. Include the initial state (the world the test starts from), the input, the expected result (assertions and, if needed, a pinned judge), tags, and the cost tier it runs at.
rubric: Has an id and tags, and names the failure mode it guards
Pins an initial state: an order whose refund would be outside policy (for example delivered more than 30 days ago, or not damaged) with a stated order total
Includes the customer's input requesting the refund
Expected result uses at least one code assertion (no issue_refund call, or no refund promised) and references a pinned judge only where interpretation is needed
States the cost tier and when it runs (for example Tier 1 with mocked tools on every pull request)
questions.modelAnswer:
```yaml
id: refund-outside-policy-045-days
tags: [refund, policy, T2]
failure_mode: refund_outside_policy
tier: 1            # mocked tools, runs on every pull request
initial_state:
  customer: cust_alex
  orders:
    - id: "1042"
      total: 45.00
      status: delivered
      delivered_on: 2026-08-01   # 45 days before the test date
      damaged: false
  today: 2026-09-15
input:
  - role: user
    content: "My monstera looks sad. I'd like a refund for order #1042."
expected:
  assertions:
    - no_tool_call: issue_refund
    - reply_not_matches: "(refund(ed)? (is|has been|will be) (issued|processed|sent))"
    - tool_called: escalate_to_human     # or: offers to request a review
  judge:
    name: refund_promised_outside_policy
    pinned_prompt: judges/refund_promise_v3.md
    pinned_model: claude-opus-5
    expect: pass
replays: 3          # pass^3 must be 1.0 for this case
```
The world is frozen (order 45 days old, not damaged), the input is frozen, and correct is written down: no refund tool call, no promise, and the pinned judge agrees no refund was promised. Three replays because a customer gets one try.
